rv.q: Williams’ experiential production conveys the corrupt value systems and ludicrous hierarchies of much of 21st-century culture with visceral force: it crushes nuance beneath Bottega Veneta heels and assaults our eyes with fake spectacle.
The performances are a marvel of speed, focus and technical adroitness.
Yet the style becomes distancing and flattens some of the subtler dimensions of their relationship
With so little variation in pacing, the exchanges begin to grind us down.
For all its alluring digital dazzle, it leaves Williams’s production rather one note and exhausting.
Instead, it feels like spending one hour and forty minutes eavesdropping on private conversations that are so trivial you wish you hadn't bothered.
In Williams’s version, it’s borderline unwatchable.
An exhilarating new satire on social media, class and how we live in unreal worlds bursts onto the Donmar stage in a frenzy of must-see vigour.
But his version is still grasping to find something more than its surface-level spectacle.
For now, though, The Maids feels like an experiment admired more than loved: a lavish, looping dream.
Later, when joined by Madame (Yerin Ha), we are treated to a masterclass in erratic petulance, spite, entitlement and ego.
This show is not. Avoid at all costs.

cn.t: Kip Williams' high-octane adaptation of Genet's classic divides critics sharply — some find its relentless, screen-driven intensity electrifying, others exhausting to the point of torment.

vr.q: I give Kip Williams adaptation of Jean Jane's The Maid five stars.
